question: Should Congress create new judgeships in the Northern District of Florida?

record.final_text:
## What the data shows — N.D. Fla. (FY2025, JB-2025, Table X-1A)

- **Weighted total filings per judgeship: 757**, against a national average of 534 (JB-2025).
- Currently has **4 authorized judgeships**.
- This is well above both benchmarks the Judicial Conference uses when it considers recommending new judgeships:
  - **430** — the standard threshold for considering an additional district judgeship (margin: +327).
  - **600** — the judicial-emergency-with-a-vacancy threshold (margin: +157), though note that whether N.D. Fla. actually *has* a judicial emergency also depends on current vacancies, which I don't have data on.
- **The Judicial Conference itself already recommended 1 additional judgeship for N.D. Fla.** in its March 2025 recommendations to Congress (JC-2025).

For context on why the caseload is so high: much of N.D. Fla.'s civil docket in recent years was driven by directly filed multidistrict litigation (e.g., MDL 2885, the 3M earplugs litigation), which inflated filings sharply starting around FY2020. That said, the weighted-filings figures above already account for case-mix weighting, not just raw counts.

## On the "should" question

Whether Congress *should* act is a policy judgment — it involves budget, politics, and factors like vacancy rates that go beyond weighted-filings data. I won't make that call. What I can say factually is:

- N.D. Fla.'s workload measure is nearly double the 430 threshold and above the 600 threshold.
- The body that studies this professionally (the Judicial Conference) has already recommended one additional judgeship for this district.

If you want, I can pull the MDL-driven filings breakdown, compare N.D. Fla. to other high-workload districts, or check how its weighted filings have trended over the past several years — any of those might help you form a view.

question: Why did federal civil filings jump in FY2020?

record.final_text:
## Federal civil filings, FY2019 → FY2020

**Official change:** civil cases filed nationwide rose from 297,877 to 470,581 — an increase of **+172,704 (+58.0%)** (Table C-1, JB-2019 → JB-2020).

### What drove it: one district, one MDL

This wasn't a broad-based increase — it was almost entirely one court and one nature-of-suit category:

- **N.D. Fla.** alone jumped from 5,107 to 204,988 filings (**+199,881**), more than the entire national increase.
- By case type, **Personal Injury/Product Liability** filings rose +184,351 nationally, almost all of it in N.D. Fla.
- The IDB-derived driver breakdown attributes **+179,741** of the change (104% of it) to **directly filed MDL cases**, dominated by **MDL 2885** (the 3M combat earplugs multidistrict litigation) centered in N.D. Fla., which added roughly +201,017 cases there on its own *(idb_derived)*.

Other large districts actually saw filings *fall*, e.g. E.D. La. (‑13,148, tied to the Taxotere/other MDL wind-downs), D.N.J. (‑5,373), and D. Ariz. (‑4,757) — meaning that excluding directly filed MDL cases, IDB-derived civil filings would have been roughly **-6,502** (i.e., slightly down) rather than up (*idb_derived*).

### Context, not causation
FY2020 also overlaps the start of the COVID-19 pandemic (national emergency declared March 13, 2020), which disrupted court operations broadly — but the data here doesn't support attributing the filings *increase* to the pandemic; the surge is explained by the MDL 2885 direct-filing wave in N.D. Fla., not COVID-related litigation *(context, our inference — not an official statement)*.

**Bottom line:** The FY2020 jump in civil filings is essentially an artifact of mass direct filing in one multidistrict litigation (earplug product-liability claims against 3M) concentrated in N.D. Fla., not a broad national trend.

question: Why did civil terminations jump in FY2024?

record.final_text:
## Civil terminations, FY2023 → FY2024

Nationally, civil cases terminated rose from 293,677 (JB-2023) to 396,635 (JB-2024) — **+102,958 (+35.1%)**, per Table C-1.

**Driver: one MDL, one district.** This jump is almost entirely attributable to N.D. Fla., which terminated 104,167 more civil cases (+37,047 → 141,214) — actually *more* than the entire national increase (104% of it), meaning other districts netted out slightly negative. That district's Personal Injury/Product Liability terminations alone rose by 104,223 cases.

By case type nationally, **Personal Injury/Product Liability** terminations rose +95,002 (92% of the total change): 66,651 → 161,653.

Digging into the IDB (idb_derived, not an official published breakdown), this is concentrated in **MDL cases**: MDL terminations overall changed by +97,266, about 94% of the national change, and the single biggest piece is **MDL 2885 in N.D. Fla. (the 3M combat earplugs litigation)**, which terminated ~102,884 more cases in FY2024 than FY2023.

Partial offsets: S.D. Fla. terminations fell −12,720 (mostly MDL 2924, the Zantac litigation, −12,699), and N.D. Ga. fell −2,454 (Personal Injury/Product Liability −3,180).

**Bottom line:** the FY2024 surge in civil terminations was overwhelmingly the courts working through the backlog of the N.D. Fla. 3M earplugs MDL (2885), which alone outweighed the entire national increase, while a partial decline in the Zantac MDL (2924, S.D. Fla.) tempered it slightly.

question: The FY2017 national civil pending count is 339,131 in one table and 366,195 in another. Why?

record.final_text:
Both figures are real — they're just from two different editions of the same official table (Table C-1, "Civil cases pending" for FY2017), and the later one is a **restatement**, not a data error:

- **339,131** — as originally published in **JB-2017** (Table C-1).
- **366,195** — the same line item as re-published in **JB-2018** (Table C-1), a restatement of the FY2017 figure.

So the jump isn't a real change in caseload between two different points in time; it's the Administrative Office revising the FY2017 pending count upward by 27,064 cases when the next year's Judicial Business volume came out (this happens periodically as case records are corrected, reclassified, or updated after the fact).

For reference, an independent rebuild from the FJC Integrated Database puts FY2017 pending at **363,601**, which is within ~0.7% of the current official 366,195 — consistent with (i.e., "matched" against) the restated JB-2018 number, not the original JB-2017 one.

**Bottom line:** use 366,195 (JB-2018) as the current official figure; 339,131 (JB-2017) is the superseded, first-published version.

question: Why did civil filings in the District of New Jersey change from FY2023 to FY2024?

record.final_text:
## D.N.J. civil filings, FY2023 → FY2024

Civil cases filed in the District of New Jersey **fell by 10,282**, from **23,871 (JB-2023, Table C-1)** to **13,589 (JB-2024, Table C-1)** — a **43.1% drop**.

**What drove it:** This was almost entirely one thing — a sharp drop-off in the Personal Injury/Product Liability category, which fell from 16,416 to 5,684 cases (−10,732), actually *more* than the total net decline (other categories moved slightly upward, offsetting some of it).

Digging into the IDB data, this traces to **directly filed MDL cases** in D.N.J.:
- **MDL 2738** (talcum powder products liability litigation) alone accounted for **−10,031** cases
- MDL 2789 (−382) and MDL 2973 (−145) contributed smaller declines

Together, changes in directly filed MDL filings account for about **104% of the total change** (idb_derived) — meaning that excluding MDL-direct cases, underlying civil filings in D.N.J. were essentially flat to slightly up (the IDB change excluding MDL-direct filings is +392).

**In short:** the apparent large decline is a filing-volume artifact of a single mass-tort MDL (talc/product liability, MDL 2738) tapering off in FY2024 after a surge in FY2023, not a broad drop in ordinary civil litigation in the district.

question: How close is the IDB reconstruction of civil cases pending in the Southern District of West Virginia on September 30, 2017 to the published figure?

record.final_text:
The IDB reconstruction is very close to the published figure — well within a "matched" tolerance.

**S.D. W. Va. — Civil cases pending, as of September 30, 2017:**
- Published (official): **71,454** (Table C-1, JB-2018 edition)
- IDB-derived reconstruction: **71,478**
- Variance: **24 cases (0.03%)**
- Status: **matched**

A couple of notes:
- The JB-2018 edition (71,454) is a large jump from the figure originally printed in JB-2017 (44,615) for the same fiscal year-end. That's a restatement between editions, not something the IDB reconciliation caused — I'm just flagging it since it's a notable revision.
- The reconciliation counts a case as "pending" if it was filed by 9/30/2017, not yet terminated by then, and (for any repeat/reopened record) its earlier termination was on or before that date — the standard rule applied here.

So at 0.03% variance, this is essentially an exact match between the case-level IDB rebuild and the official Table C-1 count.

question: How does the Eastern District of Texas's weighted caseload compare with the Judicial Conference's thresholds for new judgeships?

record.final_text:
## E.D. Tex. weighted caseload vs. Judicial Conference thresholds (FY2025, JB‑2025, Table X‑1A)

- **Weighted total filings per judgeship:** 894 — well above both thresholds
  - (Weighted civil alone: 744; authorized judgeships: 8)
- **National average, for context:** 534 — E.D. Tex. is running at roughly 1.7× the national figure

**Against the two standard benchmarks:**
| Threshold | Value | E.D. Tex. status |
|---|---|---|
| New-judgeship consideration standard | 430 | Above by 464 |
| Judicial-emergency-with-vacancy standard | 600 | Above by 294 |

Crossing 430 is the Judicial Conference's starting point for considering an additional judgeship — it isn't automatic, since the Conference also weighs senior/magistrate judge support, geography, and case mix. The 600 threshold is used only in combination with an actual vacancy to define a "judicial emergency," and this server doesn't track vacancy data, so I can't say whether E.D. Tex. currently qualifies as such.

**Bottom line:** In its March 2025 recommendations (JC-2025), the Judicial Conference did in fact recommend **2 additional judgeships** for E.D. Tex., on top of its current 8 authorized seats — consistent with its weighted filings sitting far above both the 430 and 600 benchmarks.

thresholds.label: Judicial Conference standard for considering an additional district judgeship
thresholds.description: The Judicial Conference's starting point for the district courts is 430 weighted filings per authorized judgeship after accounting for the judgeships it recommends; it generally requires a court to be above 430 to recommend an additional judgeship. It also weighs other factors (senior and magistrate judge assistance, geography, case mix), so crossing 430 is not by itself a recommendation.
thresholds.source: CRS Insight IN12541, "Recommendation for New U.S. Circuit and District Court Judgeships by the Judicial Conference of the United States (119th Congress)"; AO, "Judiciary Makes the Case for New Judgeships" (2020)

thresholds.label: Judicial emergency threshold (with a vacancy)
thresholds.description: A district court vacancy is a judicial emergency when weighted filings exceed 600 per judgeship; a vacancy open more than 18 months is an emergency when weighted filings are 430 to 600 per judgeship; so is a court with more than one authorized judgeship and only one active judge. The definition needs vacancy data, which this server doesn't have, so it can report the filings side only.
thresholds.source: Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts, "Judicial Emergency Definition"

recommendation.source: Table 1. Additional Judgeships Recommended by the Judicial Conference, 2025

data.statement: E.D. Tex. had 894 weighted filings per authorized judgeship in FY2025 (JB-2025, Table X-1A), above the 430 and 600 thresholds. In 2025 the Judicial Conference recommended 2 additional judgeships for it. This server makes no recommendation of its own.

provenance.series: Judicial Business of the United States Courts
provenance.definition: Weighted civil plus weighted criminal plus weighted supervised release hearings, divided by authorized judgeships. The Judicial Conference generally considers new judgeships above 430 and treats above 600 as a judicial emergency threshold (see CRS Insight IN12541).

provenance.series: Judicial Conference of the United States
provenance.definition: Additional judgeships recommended by the Judicial Conference.
